gloss: Any piece of content in a game: images, sounds, music, 3D models, fonts.
A 2D image used for a character or object, often with several frames for animation.
A sheet of small square images (tiles) you arrange on a grid to build levels.
Software that handles drawing, physics, input and sound so you can focus on your game (e.g. Godot, Unity).
The cycle every game repeats: read input, update the world, draw the screen — many times per second.
The main thing the player does over and over, like jump–collect–avoid.
A quick, rough version made to test if an idea is fun.
Minimum viable product: the smallest version you could actually release.
When two objects touch; engines detect it so you can react (lose a life, pick up a coin).
The invisible shape used to check collisions, often simpler than the art.
One screen or area of a game, with its objects.
Code attached to an object that tells it how to behave.
A named value the game remembers, like score or lives.
A message that something happened (button pressed, enemy hit) that code can react to.
How many times per second the screen updates. 60 is common.
Turning your project into something others can play (a web page, an app, an .exe).
Watching someone else play your game to find what’s confusing or broken.
Making software by describing what you want to an AI assistant and refining its output.
The instructions you type to an AI assistant.
A whole game in one .html file that runs in any browser.
A 3D style with few polygons — simple, fast and beginner-friendly.
Art drawn pixel by pixel at small sizes, scaled up for a retro look.
A common open file format for 3D models, supported by Blender and Godot.
A public-domain style license: use the asset for anything, no credit needed.
A Creative Commons license: free to use if you credit the creator.
Like CC BY but non-commercial: you can’t use it in something you sell.
Software whose code is public and free to use, change and share under its license.
Free to start, with paid upgrades.
An event where people make a game in a short time, often around a theme.

faq: I’ve never made anything. Where do I start?
Open the Start here page, pick your age group, and follow the three steps. Plan a tiny game first — one action, one way to win, one way to lose.
Do I need to know how to code?
No. Scratch, MakeCode Arcade, Roblox Studio templates and AI assistants let you start without writing code from scratch. Learning a little code later helps a lot.
Is it really free?
Many great tools are free, including Godot, Blender, Scratch and Audacity. Filter the tools directory by “free”. Always check the official site — prices change.
What age can my kid start?
Many kids start around 6–8 with Scratch or similar block tools, with a grown-up nearby. Check each tool’s age rules; several AI chatbots require 13+ or 18+.
Which engine should I pick?
For a first 2D game, Godot is free and beginner-friendly. If you already play Roblox or Fortnite, their creator tools are a fun start. Don’t overthink it — finishing a small game matters more.
Can AI make the whole game for me?
AI can write a working small game, especially a single HTML file, but you still decide what’s fun, test it, and fix problems. Think of it as a fast helper.
How long does a first game take?
A tiny game can take a weekend. Keep the plan small and add features in version 2.
Where do I get art and sound?
Use free libraries like Kenney (CC0) and Freesound (check each sound’s license), or make your own. See our free art and free sound pages.
Can I sell my game?
Usually yes, if every asset you used allows commercial use and you follow each tool’s terms. Avoid CC BY-NC assets in paid games.
How do I share my game?
For web games, itch.io and GitHub Pages are free. See the “Publish on itch.io” tutorial.
Is this site sponsored?
Sponsor slots are clearly labeled. Listings and recommendations are not paid placements.
Does Build Buddy send my messages anywhere?
No. Build Buddy runs entirely in your browser and only uses this site’s own data. Nothing you type leaves your device.
